newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine central bank hopes rate hike will calm market.
newsitem.headline: Philippine central bank hopes rate hike will calm market.

text.p: The Philippine Central Bank said on Friday its latest hikes in overnight lending rates should calm financial markets, but warned that it may take more drastic steps if peso speculation does not die down.
The peso has been hit by speculation arising from attacks on the Thai baht.
"We're not saying this is our last move. Hopefully, this will calm the market," Central Bank Treasurer Sergio Edeza told Reuters.
The Philippine Central Bank started offering three-day reverse repos at 20 percent on Friday, which effectively raises the overnight borrowing rate to 20 from 13 percent, Edeza said.
Edeza added the overnight lending rate was also being lifted simultaneously to 21 from 14 percent.
In two days, the central bank has increased its overnight borrowing rate by a total of 8.75 percentage points to protect the peso.
Traders said the overnight rates are now the highest since March 1995, when they rose to 30 percent as the government defended the peso following the Mexican economic crisis.

The Philippine peso rose to 26.368 to the dollar in midsession on Friday after opening at its low of 26.375. Traders said banks were forced to sell dollars after the central bank move on the three-day reverse repo rate.
The Philippines pounced on speculators on Thursday, hoping to prevent Thailand's financial troubles spreading to its own markets, but not all analysts were convinced it would work.
The central bank raised interest rates twice during the day and dumped more than $70 million in the morning to protect the peso.
The government insists that after five years of consistent growth the bad old days in mismanagement and boom-bust cycles are over.

But analysts said Manila still had to prove itself to the investor community, already appearing jaded about the fortunes of southeast Asia at a time when the Philippines is only just beginning to catch up.

The Manila share index shed 54.96 points, or 2.09 percent, to close at a year-low of 2,576.13 points on Friday as local investors remained wary of a spillover from battered Thai markets, brokers said.
"People are still affected by negative sentiment triggered by Thailand's baht. The preferred position right now is to be liquid," said Dennis Rayala, research head at Abacus Securities.
Talk of a possible baht devaluation over the past few days had battered the Thai stock market and the currency.
But the baht has rallied since Wednesday following intervention by the central bank and assurances by Thai authorities that it would not devalue the currency.
